Story: There was once, in a barn adjacent to a farmhouse, a small white kitten called Cotton. Cotton resided high above the barn in a warm and comfortable nook where the farmer's horses were accustomed to sleep. Yet Cotton was not solitary in her abode above the barn. She shared her bed of hay with her mother and 5 other sisters. All her sisters were pleasing and fluffy, resembling Cotton in appearance. But she was the sole white kitten among them. The remainder of her sisters were entirely orange, marked with fine white tiger stripes such as Cotton's mother possessed. Her difference of appearance caused Cotton considerable sorrow. She frequently desired to resemble the rest of her family. Thus, upon one day, when Cotton discovered a can of orange paint belonging to the farmer, she employed it to colour herself in imitation of them. When her mother and sisters came upon her, they began to laugh.

"What are you doing, Cotton?!"

"I only wanted to be more like you".

Cotton's mother rubbed her face upon Cotton's and said, "Oh Cotton, but your fur is so pretty and special, like you. We would never want you to be any other way". Thereupon, Cotton's mother lifted her and cast her into a large bucket of water. When Cotton emerged, she was once more herself. Her sisters licked her face until Cotton's fur was entirely dry.

"Don't ever do that again, Cotton!" they all cried. "Next time you might mess up that pretty white fur of yours and we wouldn't want that!"

Thereupon Cotton reflected, "I change my mind. I like being special".

Question: What color was Cotton?
Answer:

Story: There was once a beautiful fish named Asta, who inhabited the ocean. The ocean wherein Asta dwelt was home to numerous other fish; together, they passed their days in play.

Upon a certain day, a bottle floated above the heads of Asta and his companions. They gazed upward and beheld the bottle. "What is it?" inquired Sharkie, a friend of Asta. "It looks like a bird's belly," replied Asta. Yet, as they swam nearer, it proved not to be a bird's belly; it was hard and transparent, and contained something within.

The bottle remained suspended above them. Eager to discover its contents, they seized the bottle and bore it down to the ocean's floor. Upon a rock, they fractured it open. Once opened, they discovered what lay within: it was a note, inscribed in orange crayon upon white paper. Neither Asta nor Sharkie could decipher the note, so they conveyed it to Asta's papa. "What does it say?" they inquired.

Asta's papa perused the note. He addressed Asta and Sharkie, saying, "This note is from a little girl. She wants to be your friend. If you want to be her friend, we can write a note to her. But you have to find another bottle so we can send it to her." And so it was done.

Story: (CNN) -- On Friday evening, agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation searched the Maryland residence of the suspect in the recent disappearance of an American woman in Aruba, as an agent reported.

The search took place at the Gaithersburg residence of Gary Giordano, who is at present detained in an Aruban jail; this was informed by FBI Special Agent Rich Wolf to CNN.

Agents arrived at about 8:40 p.m. on Friday, wearing vests inscribed with 'FBI' and bearing empty cardboard and plastic boxes. Approximately 15 unmarked cars were observable upon the street, together with a vehicle of the Montgomery County police.

Supervisory Special Agent Philip Celestini, present at the residence, declined to offer further comment upon the search, citing the active investigation.

Aruban Solicitor General Taco Stein stated earlier on Friday that the suspect is to appear in court on Monday, where an investigating magistrate might order him to be held for at least eight additional days, to remain upon the island, or to be released outright for want of evidence.

Giordano was apprehended by Aruban police on August 5, three days subsequent to the last sighting of Robyn Gardner near Baby Beach on the western extremity of the Caribbean island.

Giordano informed authorities that he had been snorkeling with Gardner when he signaled to her to return to shore; upon reaching the beach, Gardner was nowhere to be found, as Giordano allegedly stated.

The area to which Giordano led authorities is a rocky and unsightly place, which, according to locals, is not a popular spot for snorkeling.

Although prosecutors have persisted in identifying the 50-year-old American man by his initials, GVG, they have also released a photograph of a man who appears to be Giordano. His attorney, Michael Lopez, has likewise stated that his client is detained as a suspect in Gardner's death. Lopez has not returned telephone calls made in request of comment.

Story: Tommy was a small boy who lived by a big lake by the woods. On a certain day, he observed two little mice gazing at the water. They appeared exceedingly sorrowful. 

"What is wrong?" Tommy asked. 

Mary, one of the little mice, stood. "My brother and I love to see new things. We want to see what is on the other side of the lake. But we do not know how to build a boat to get there." 

Tommy smiled. "I have plenty of toy boats," he said. "They are your size!" 

"Oh, thank you!" said Steve, the other little mouse. "We would be very glad if we could borrow it!" 

Tommy proceeded to his dwelling and came back with a small toy boat. The boat was furnished with a large sail to propel it. Mary and Steve boarded it, and Tommy placed the boat upon the water. 

The boat sailed away across the water. Mary and Steve laughed with joy and experienced great enjoyment in riding the toy boat. 

Before long, they arrived at the opposite shore of the lake. A great many people were enjoying themselves by swimming and splashing in the water. Steve and Mary were delighted to observe all the new things and persons. 

A man cast a ball into the water. It fell near the toy boat. The man's large dog came splashing into the water to retrieve it. The great waves splashed the little boat in every direction. Mary and Steve became exceedingly wet. 

Mary and Steve returned home thereafter. They recounted to Tommy all that they had seen, and they all laughed at the great waves made by the dog. On the morrow, the mice would explore further upon the lake with Tommy's toy boat!

Question: Where'd Tommy live?

Story: Brownie and Spotty, neighbouring dogs, met each day to play together. These two were so attached to one another and played together with such frequency that a path had been worn through the grass of the field between their respective houses. One evening, Brownie's family observed that he had not returned home. They went in search of him without success; by the next week, he was still missing. Curiously, Spotty appeared at Brownie's house alone, barking, whining, and generally pestering Brownie's human family. Being occupied with their own affairs, they merely ignored the anxious little neighbour dog. Ted, Brownie's owner, was constantly disturbed by the angry, determined little dog. Spotty followed Ted about, barking insistently, and then rushing toward a nearby empty lot and back, as if to say, "Follow me! It's urgent!" At length, Ted followed Spotty to a deserted spot, half a mile from the house. There Ted found his beloved Brownie alive, with one of his hind legs crushed in a steel leghold trap. Horrified, Ted now wished that he had taken Spotty's earlier appeals seriously. Then Ted noticed something quite remarkable. Spotty had done more than merely lead Brownie's human owner to his trapped friend. In a circle around the injured dog, Ted discovered an array of dog food and table scraps, which were afterwards identified as the remains of every meal with which Spotty had been fed that week! Spotty had been visiting Brownie regularly, in the hope of keeping his friend alive by the sacrifice of his own comfort. Spotty had evidently stayed with Brownie to protect him from hunger and other perils, and to keep up his spirits. Brownie's leg was treated by a veterinarian, and he recovered. For many years thereafter, the two families watched the faithful friends chasing each other down that well-worn path between their houses.

Story: CHAPTER FIFTY FIVE. 

WAITING. 

The days, lengthening in the sunlight, continued without bringing either that which Romola most desired or that which she most dreaded. No sign came from Baldassarre, and despite the vigilant watch of the Government, no disclosure of the suspected conspiracy was made. Yet other events occurred which affected her deeply, and spanned the spectre-haunted interval of anxiety with active sympathy in present affliction. There came the spreading Plague and the Excommunication of Savonarola. 

These two events served to stay her nascent alienation from the Frate, and to renew her attachment to the man who had disclosed to her the new life of duty, and who now appeared worsted in the struggle of principle against profligacy. For it was not possible for Romola to bear, from day to day, into the dwellings of pestilence and misery, the exalted emotion of a joy that, inasmuch as such anguish endured, she also endured to render some of the bitterness less acute, without recollecting that she owed this sublime moral existence to Fra Girolamo. She could not behold the silencing and excommunication of a man whose difference from the general body of the clergy lay, not in heretical doctrine, nor in his superstitions, but in the fervour with which he endeavoured to render the Christian life real, without feeling herself powerfully attracted to his cause. 

Late in the fervid days of June, the Excommunication, which had arrived from Rome some weeks before, was formally promulgated in the Duomo. Romola repaired to the scene, that the resistance it awakened might strengthen that sympathy with Savonarola which constituted one source of her strength. It presented a memorable contrast to that which she had been wont to behold in that place.

Story: NEW YORK (CNN) -- Natasha Richardson, a film star, Tony-winning stage actress, and member of the famed Redgrave acting family, died on Wednesday after suffering injuries in a ski accident, according to a family statement. She was 45.

Natasha Richardson fell on a beginners' slope in Canada.

Richardson, wife of the actor Liam Neeson, was injured on Monday in a fall on a ski slope at a Quebec resort situated about 80 miles northwest of Montreal.

Richardson's family released a statement saying, "Liam Neeson, his sons, and the entire family are shocked and devastated by the tragic death of their beloved Natasha. They are profoundly grateful for the support, love and prayers of everyone, and ask for privacy during this very difficult time."

According to a statement issued by Mont Tremblant Ski Resort, Richardson fell during a lesson on a beginners' trail. Watch a report on Richardson's life »

"She did not show any visible sign of injury, but the ski patrol followed strict procedures and brought her back to the bottom of the slope and insisted she should see a doctor," the statement said.

Richardson, who was accompanied by her instructor, returned to her hotel; but about an hour after the fall she was "not feeling good," the statement said. An ambulance was summoned, and Richardson was conveyed to a local hospital before being transferred to Hopital du Sacre-Coeur in Montreal. From that institution she was transferred to Lenox Hill Hospital in New York City.

Friends and colleagues were saddened by her death.

"Natasha was brilliant, beautiful, funny, talented beyond measure, as emotionally raw as she was razor sharp," said Jodie Foster, who had worked with Richardson in "Nell," in a statement. "Tasha loved fiercely and that love continues in all of us who knew her. May Liam, her beautiful boys and her loving family hold her close as they move through this tragic moment."

On the third day following his arrival at the camp, Archie received orders to make ready to set forth with the hound, accompanied by the earl and a considerable company of men-at-arms, in quest of Bruce. A traitor had but recently come in and disclosed the place where Bruce had lain the night before. Archie, with reluctance, unfastened the chain from the pole and, holding the end in his hand, proceeded with Hector to the front of the pavilion. He was resolved that if, under the guidance of the dog, the party should draw near to Bruce, he would slay the dog and then attempt to escape by speed of foot; though of this, as there were so many mounted men in the company, he entertained but slender hope. Led by the peasant, they made their way to the hut, which lay five miles distant in the hills. Upon reaching it, Hector at once became exceedingly excited. He sniffed here and there, hunted eagerly up and down the cottage, then made a circuit round it, and at last, with a loud and deep bay, he started off with his nose to the ground, pulling so hard upon the chain that Archie had much ado to keep pace with him. Pembroke and his knights rode a little in the rear, followed by their men-at-arms. 

"I pray you, Sir Earl," Archie said, "keep not too close to my traces, for the sound of the horse's hoofs and the jingling of the equipments make him all the more impatient to get forward, and even now it taxes all my strength to hold him in."

Story: Chapter 17: The Battle Of Moncontor.

When Pierre left him in order to look after the horses, Philip continued his meal; for there could be no hurry, since Nevers was twelve miles away, and it would be four hours, at least, before a party could arrive from that place.

It was the landlady herself who brought in the next course; and after placing the dish upon the table, she stood looking earnestly at him for a minute, then said:

"You spoke of stopping here tonight, sir. The accommodation is very poor and, if you will take my advice, you will ride farther. There have been some men along here this afternoon, inquiring for a party like yours; and offering a reward to any who would carry the news to them, should you pass through. Methinks their intentions were not friendly."

"I thank you very much for your counsel," Philip said, "and will take it. I know that there are some who would gladly hinder me, in my journey; and if there is, as you say, a risk of their coming here for me, it were as well that I rode farther, although I would gladly have given my horses a night's rest. I thank you warmly for having warned me."

"Do not let my husband know that I have spoken to you," she said. "He is an honest man, but timid; and in these days 'tis safest not to meddle with what does not concern one."

Having waited for two hours, Philip then told Pierre to saddle the horses, and to inform the landlord that he wished to speak with him.

F. T. PALGRAVE.

When Anne Woodford began to wake from the constant thought of the grief and horror she had left at Portchester, and to feel more alive to her surroundings, less as if they were a kind of dream in which she only mechanically took her part, one thing impressed itself on her gradually; and that was disappointment. If the previous shock had not blunted all her hopes and aspirations, perhaps she would have felt it sooner and more keenly; but she could not help realising that she had put herself into an inferior position, whence there did not seem to be the promotion she had once anticipated. Her companion rockers were of an inferior grade to herself. Jane Humphreys was a harmless but silly girl, not much wiser, though less spoilt, than poor little Madam, and full of Cockney vulgarities. Education was unfashionable just then, and though Hester Bridgeman was better born and bred, being the daughter of an attorney in the city, she was not much better instructed, and had no pursuits except that of her own advantage. Pauline Dunord was by far the best of the three; but she seemed to live a life apart, taking very little interest in her companions or anything around her, except her devotions and the bringing them over to her Church. The nursery was quite a separate establishment; there was no mingling with the guests of royalty, who were only seen in excited peeps from the window, or when solemnly introduced to the presence chamber to pay their respects to the Prince. As to books, the only secular one that Anne saw while at Whitehall was an odd volume of Parthenissa. The late King's summary of the Roman controversy was to be had in plenty; and nothing was more evident than that the only road to favour or promotion was in being thereby convinced.

Story: CHAPTER III

TOM'S JOKE

"What did you do to him?" Sam inquired with promptness.

"Put an advertisement of pills on his back and some other ads. in his text books," Tom replied. "Say, he looks some mad; doesn't he?"

"I should say yes," Stanley affirmed.

At that moment, William Philander advanced with rapid strides; in one hand he bore the poster which Tom had affixed to his back, and with the other he shook his fist in great wrath.

"Tom Rover, you've--er--insulted me!" he gasped upon approaching. "You've humiliated me before the whole class! I'll--I'll----" The dandy, being consumed by rage, found himself unable to speak.

"Take a cough drop and clear your throat Billy," Tom suggested calmly. "Don't get so excited, you might drop dead from heart disease."

"How dare you put that--er--that advertisement of Gumley's Red Pills on my back?" the fashionably dressed one stormed.

"'Gumley's Red Pills for Red-Blooded People,'" Spud quoted from the poster. "Say, they are fine, Willie. Didn't you ever take 'em?"

"No, and I don't want to. I want Tom Ro----"

"Say, if you haven't taken any of Gumley's pills you don't know what you've missed," Spud continued, with a wink at the others. "Why, there was a man over in Rottenberg who was flat on his back with half a dozen fatal diseases. The doctors gave him just three days to live,--three days, think of it! His wife nearly cried her eyes out. Then along came this Gumley man with a trunk full of his Red Pills for Red-Blooded People. He didn't exactly know if the dying man was red-blooded or not, but he took a chance and gave the fellow sixteen pills, four after breakfast, four after dinner, four after supper and four on retiring, and the next day, what do you think happened? That man got up and went to work, and he's been at his Job ever since."

Story: CHAPTER V.

MESSRS. TREAT, JONES, WESTON & DOWD.

The particular circle of society in which Ben and Johnny moved was shaken to its very centre by the news which was whispered from one to another on the day after those young gentlemen and Paul had taken up their abode at Mrs. Green's. Early that morning the most exciting topic of conversation had been Master Spry's misfortune and Tim Dooley's perfidy; and that had hardly begun to be commented upon when the news spread that Ben and Johnny, since the coming of their guest, who was evidently a suspicious sort of person, as was shown by his clothes and his entire ignorance of the slang of the street, were no longer proud of their neat little bit of real estate, but had made a change which would probably be the means of their financial ruin. That they had been so extravagant as to engage rooms at a regular boarding-house, where they were to spend their substance on three square meals each day, seemed like a reckless disregard of money; and the price which they were to pay for board was stated at various sums from five to ten dollars per week. But that was not the only bit of wonderful news. Jimmy Sullivan stated-and he was supported by several others as the time wore on-that Johnny himself had told him that they were to start a regular theatre, and had already engaged a hall, which would be converted into a first-class place of amusement as soon as possible. This would have been regarded simply as a rumour started for the purpose of injuring the credit of these young gentlemen, had it not come so directly from one of the parties concerned, and must therefore be true. 

Final question:
Question: Who started to live at Mrs Green's?
Answer:

Story: CHAPTER XII

"Throw your coat down anywhere, Miss Baldwin," Wingate invited, as he ushered that young lady into his rooms soon after eleven o'clock on the following evening. "Now what can I give you? There are some sandwiches here--ham and pâté-de-foie-gras, I think. Whisky and soda or some hock?"

"A pâté sandwich and some plain soda water, please," Sarah replied, removing the long motoring coat which concealed her evening clothes. "I have been fined for everything except disorderly driving--daren't risk that. Thanks!" she added. "What ripping sandwiches! And quite a good play, wasn't it?"

"I am glad you enjoyed it."

"It was a swindle Josephine not turning up," Sarah continued, stretching herself out in Wingate's easy-chair. "Domestic ructions again, I suppose. How I do hate that husband of hers!"

"It was disappointing," he admitted.

There ensued a brief pause, during which Sarah finished her sandwiches and lit a cigarette.

"Wilshaw seems to be having a little trouble with the outside porter," her host remarked presently.

"It must cost him at least half a sovereign every time I leave the cab," Sarah sighed.

"How much do you make a week out of your driving, if it isn't too personal a question?" he enquired.

"It depends upon how much Jimmy's got."

"Is he your only client, then?"

"He very seldom gives me a chance of another. Once or twice I've refused to be engaged by the day, but he sends his man around to the garage and I find him sitting in the cab when I arrive."

"A pâté sandwich and some plain soda water, please," Sarah replied, taking off the long motoring coat which concealed her evening clothes. "I have been fined for everything except disorderly driving--daren't risk that. Thanks!" she went on. "What ripping sandwiches! And quite a good play, wasn't it?" 

"I am glad you enjoyed it." 

"It was a swindle Josephine not turning up," Sarah continued, as she stretched herself out in Wingate's easy-chair. "Domestic ructions again, I suppose. How I do hate that husband of hers!" 

"It was disappointing," he admitted.

There ensued a brief pause, during which Sarah finished her sandwiches and lit a cigarette.

"Wilshaw seems to be having a little trouble with the outside porter," her host remarked presently.

"It must cost him at least half a sovereign every time I leave the cab," Sarah sighed.

"How much do you make a week out of your driving, if it isn't too personal a question?" he enquired.

"It depends upon how much Jimmy's got."

"Is he your only client, then?"

"He very seldom gives me a chance of another. Once or twice I've refused to be engaged by the day, but he sends his man around to the garage and I find him sitting in the cab when I arrive."

"Throw your coat down anywhere, Miss Baldwin," Wingate invited, as he conducted the young lady into his apartments shortly after eleven o'clock upon the following evening. "Now what can I give you? There are some sandwiches here--ham and pâté-de-foie-gras, I think. Whisky and soda or some hock?" 

"A pâté sandwich and some plain soda water, please," Sarah replied, removing the lengthy motoring coat that concealed her evening attire. "I have been fined for everything except disorderly driving--daren't risk that. Thanks!" she added. "What ripping sandwiches! And quite a good play, wasn't it?" 

"I am glad you enjoyed it." 

"It was a swindle Josephine not turning up," Sarah continued, as she reclined in Wingate's easy-chair. "Domestic ructions again, I suppose. How I do hate that husband of hers!" 

"It was disappointing," he admitted. 

A brief pause ensued, during which Sarah consumed her sandwiches and ignited a cigarette. 

"Wilshaw seems to be having a little trouble with the outside porter," her host remarked presently. 

"It must cost him at least half a sovereign every time I leave the cab," Sarah sighed. 

"How much do you make a week out of your driving, if it isn't too personal a question?" he enquired. 

"It depends upon how much Jimmy's got." 

"Is he your only client, then?" 

"He very seldom gives me a chance of another. Once or twice I've refused to be engaged by the day, but he sends his man around to the garage and I find him sitting in the cab when I arrive."

Story: A comprehensive grasp of adolescence in society requires information from a great many perspectives, such as psychology, biology, history, sociology, education, and anthropology. In each of these views, adolescence is considered a transitional period between childhood and adulthood, whose cultural purpose is to prepare children for the roles of adults. It is a period of numerous transitions, encompassing education, training, employment and unemployment, as well as changes from one living circumstance to another.

Puberty unfolds through a protracted process, commencing with a surge in the production of hormones, which in turn occasions a variety of physical changes. It is that stage of life marked by the appearance and development of secondary sex characteristics-such as a deeper voice and a larger adam's apple in boys, and the growth of breasts and more curved, prominent hips in girls-and a pronounced shift in the hormonal balance towards an adult state. This development is initiated by the pituitary gland, which secretes a flood of hormonal agents into the bloodstream, thereby setting in motion a chain reaction. The male and female gonads are thereafter activated, placing them in a state of rapid growth and development; the stimulated gonads now commence the mass production of the requisite chemicals. The testes principally release testosterone, whereas the ovaries predominantly dispense estrogen. The production of these hormones rises gradually until sexual maturation is attained. In some cases, boys may develop gynecomastia on account of an imbalance in sex hormones, tissue responsiveness, or obesity.

Story: CHAPTER XX.

Moving Against Captain Grady

Both Paul and Chet Winthrop were deeply interested in the words uttered by Jeff Jones, the colored member of the horse thieves' gang.

"So you know something of Captain Grady and our uncle, Barnaby Winthrop?" cried Chet, excitedly. "What do you know?"

"Dat's fer you two fellers ter find out--onless yer let's me go," replied Jeff Jones, suggestively.

"You mean you won't speak unless we grant you your liberty?" put in Paul.

"Dat's de way to figure it."

Paul looked at Chet inquiringly.

"We can't promise anything until Mr. Dottery gets back," said Chet. "But if you know anything about our uncle you had better speak out, if you wish us to do anything at all for you."

"I won't say a word," growled the colored man.

Chet bit his lip in vexation.

"Don't you know what it is to have us able to speak a word for you?" said Paul. "Supposing we let Jack Blowfen take you over to the next camp and tell the men that you are a downright horse thief? Would you fancy that?"

She came round with a lashing of canvas, extended seaward, and returned with her deck sharply inclined and small puffs of bitter spray blowing over her weather rail, for it was certain that the breeze was freshening apace. Thereupon Dampier sent a man aloft into the foremast shrouds, and thereafter regarded Wyllard.

Story: CHAPTER XXVIII. 

A MEETING. 

Approximately a week after the dissolution of the Crooked Creek Company, Harry was riding from Hetertown and had nearly reached the creek on his homeward journey when he encountered George Purvis. 

This constituted their first meeting since the fight, as George had been absent on a visit to relatives in Richmond. 

Upon perceiving George riding slowly toward him, Harry felt exceedingly embarrassed and was vexed by his own embarrassment. 

How ought he to meet George? What should he say, or should he say anything at all? 

He did not wish to appear anxious to "make up" with him, nor did he desire to seem as though he bore malice toward him. If only he knew how George felt about the matter! 

As it was, he wished that he had stopped somewhere upon the road. He had thought of stopping at the mill; why had he not done so? That would have given George time to pass by. 

Both boys appeared to be riding as slowly as their horses would consent to go; yet, when they met, Harry had not half made up his mind what he would say, or how he should say it, or whether it would be better to say anything at all. 

"Hello, George!" said he, quite without premeditation. 

"Hello!" said George, reining in his horse. "Where are you going?" 

"Going home," said Harry, also stopping in the road. 

Thus was the quarrel brought to an end. 

"So you've sold the telegraph?" said George. 

"Yes," said Harry. "And I think we made a pretty good bargain. I didn't think we'd do so well when we started."

Story: CHAPTER VI.—LEO ASSERTS HIS RIGHTS. 

A crowd of performers at once surrounded the pair; as few of them were fond of Jack Snipper, they wondered what Leo would do should the gymnast attack the boy. 

“Call me a braggart, will you!” roared Snipper. 

“Don’t you dare to touch me with that club!” replied Leo calmly. 

“I’ll teach you a lesson!” 

Whereupon, swinging the Indian club above his head, Jack Snipper struck a savage blow at the young gymnast. 

Had the club struck Leo, the boy’s head would have sustained a severe injury. 

However, Leo dodged with great quickness, and the Indian club passed harmlessly through the air. 

“For shame, Snipper!” 

“Do you want to kill the boy?” 

“What harm has he done?” 

Thus the cries continued. 

“Mind your own affairs!” shouted the maddened gymnast. “I’m going to teach the boy a lesson!” 

Again he sprang at Leo. 

But suddenly the Indian club was caught. With a dexterous twist, it was sent flying out of reach across the dressing tent. 

Then, before Snipper could recover, he received a stinging slap full in the face, which sent him staggering backward upon the grass. 

A shout of approval arose. 

“Good for Leo!” 

“That’s right, boy, stand up for your rights!” 

The shout summoned Adam Lambert, the general manager, to the scene. 

No sooner had he appeared than all the performers departed. It was contrary to the rules to fight, and every person present was liable to a heavy fine.

Story: Zen (), a school of Mahayana Buddhism, had its origin in China during the Tang dynasty, where it was termed Chan Buddhism. The Zen school was powerfully influenced by Taoism and evolved as a separate school of Chinese Buddhism. From China, Chan Buddhism extended southward to Vietnam, northeastward to Korea, and eastward to Japan, in which country it received the name Japanese Zen. 

The term Zen is derived from the Japanese pronunciation of the Middle Chinese word 禪 (Chan), which traces its origin to the Indian practice of Dhyana ("meditation"). Zen emphasizes rigorous self-control, the practice of meditation, insight into Buddha-nature, and the personal expression of this insight in daily life, with particular regard to the benefit of others. As a consequence, it sets less store upon mere knowledge of sutras and doctrine, and favors direct understanding through zazen and intercourse with an accomplished teacher. 

The teachings of Zen embrace various sources of Mahayana thought, more especially Yogachara, the Tathāgatagarbha sūtras, and the Huayan school, with their emphasis upon Buddha-nature, totality, and the Bodhisattva-ideal. The Prajñāpāramitā literature, and, to a lesser degree, Madhyamaka, have likewise been influential in the shaping of the "paradoxical language" of the Zen-tradition. 

The word "Zen" is derived from the Japanese pronunciation of the Middle Chinese word 禪 () (pinyin: "Chán"), which is itself derived from the Sanskrit word "dhyāna" (ध्यान ), a term that may be rendered, with approximate fidelity, as "absorption" or "meditative state".

Lodovico had detached himself from the league and again made terms with France, for his own safety's sake. But his cousin, Giovanni Sforza, Tyrant of Pesaro, the husband of Lucrezia Borgia, continued in the pontifical army at the head of a condotta of 600 lances. Another command in the same ranks was one of 700 lances under the youthful Giuffredo Borgia, now Prince of Squillace and the husband of Doña Sancia of Aragon, a lady of exceedingly loose morals, who had brought to Rome the habits acquired in the most licentious Court of that licentious age.

The French lost Naples even more easily than they had conquered it, and by July 7 Ferdinand II was able to reenter his capital and reascend his throne. D'Aubigny, the French general, withdrew to France; whilst Montpensier, the Viceroy, retired to Pozzuoli, where he died in the following year.

Janet could find but four eggs in the chicken pen. She looked under every chicken, and in every nest, yet could not discover another egg. "Quack" said a nearby duck, as Janet took an egg from the nest. Now she had enough for breakfast.

It seemed that every person who had doubted Sam's honesty deemed it essential to visit Mrs. Byram's and congratulate him upon what now appeared to be substantial evidence of his innocence. 

Fred and the miners likewise received their share of attention; and even Bill, whose limb pained him severely, joined his partners in celebrating a victory that now appeared assured. 

Prior to returning home, Mr. Hunter called to confer with his clients regarding the formation of a stock company for the new mine; and, when he departed, he did so with full authority to act as he believed their interests required. 

Among the evening's visitors was Donovan, and he did not hesitate to reprove himself harshly for having been so foolish as to suppose that his old friends might have been involved in any dubious affair. 

"The cashier is about as sore a man as can be found in town," he said, "an' if I ain't way off in my reckonin' he'll be lookin' for another job mighty soon." 

"Does he say anything against us?" Bill asked. 

"He's glum as a fish. Every feller who goes in wants to know where Gus is, an' he keeps out of sight all that's possible." 

"Have you seen Mr. Wright to-day?" 

"No; but I heard he an' that lawyer of yours had a long chin about the business. Say, Bill, by the time you get out of this scrape you'll owe a pretty penny for law, I reckon. Why don't you try to make the company pay it?"

Story: CHAPTER XX

A BLIZZARD

A bitter wind searched the poplar bluff where George and his hired man, Grierson, were cutting fuel. Trees of any size are scarce upon the prairie, except in the river valleys; but the slender trunks and leafless branches were closely massed, and afforded a little shelter. Outside upon the open waste, the cold was almost too severe to face, and George once or twice glanced anxiously across the snowy levels, looking for some sign of Edgar, who should have joined them with the team and sledge. It was, however, difficult to see far, for a gray dimness narrowed in the horizon. George stood in the center of a little clearing strewn with rows of fallen trunks from which he was hewing off the branches, dressed in snow-flecked furs. The work was hard; his whole body strained with each stroke of the heavy ax, but it failed to keep him warm, and the wind was growing more bitter with the approach of night.

"I don't know what can be keeping West," he said after a while. "We haven't seen the mail-carrier either, and he's two hours late; but he must have had a heavy trail all the way from the settlement. I expect he'll cut out our place and make straight for Grant's. We'll have snow before long."

Not far away there stood an empty shack where, by George's consent, the mail-carrier left letters when bad weather made it desirable to shorten his round.

Grierson nodded as he glanced about. The stretch of desolate white prairie had contracted since he had last noticed it; the surrounding dimness was creeping nearer in, and the ranks of poplar trunks were losing their sharpness of form. Now that the men had ceased chopping, they could hear the eerie moaning of the wind and the sharp patter of icy snow-dust among the withered brush.

Story: CHAPTER VIII. BRUCE AND THE WAR OF INDEPENDENCE.

The position of Edward I towards France made it, in fact, more desirable for him that Scotland should be independent and friendly than half subdued and hostile to his rule. While she was hostile, England, in attacking France, always left an enemy in her rear. Edward supposed, however, that by clemency to all the Scottish leaders except Wallace, by giving them great appointments and trusting them fully, and by calling them to his Parliament in London, he could combine England and Scotland in affectionate union. He repaired the ruins of war in Scotland; he began to study her laws and customs; he hastily ran up for her a new constitution, and appointed his nephew, John of Brittany, as governor. But he had overlooked two facts: the Scottish clergy, from the highest to the lowest, were irreconcilably opposed to union with England; and the greatest and most warlike of the Scottish nobles, if not patriotic, were fickle and insatiably ambitious. It is hard to reckon how often Robert Bruce had turned his coat, and how often the Bishop of St Andrews had taken the oath to Edward. Both men were in Edward's favour in June 1304, but in that month they made against him a treasonable secret covenant. Through 1305 Bruce prospered in Edward's service; on February 10, 1306, Edward was conferring on him a new favour, little guessing that Bruce, after some negotiation with his old rival, the Red Comyn, had slain him (an uncle of his was also butchered) before the high altar of the Church of the Franciscans in Dumfries. Apparently Bruce had tried to enlist Comyn in his conspiracy, and had found him recalcitrant, or feared that he would be treacherous (February 10, 1306).

Story: Luna, the hawk, desired a pair of socks. It was the depth of winter, and perching upon tree branches rendered her feet exceedingly cold. Luna trusted that her friends might assist her in obtaining some socks. She took flight to the ancient maple tree wherein Olive the owl made her abode. 

"Olive, may I please borrow a pair of your socks?" she asked. 

Olive the owl looked surprised. "Luna, I have no use for socks because my legs and toes have thick feathers. Go visit one of the animals that walk on four legs. They might have extra socks you could borrow." 

Luna flew across the field and alighted beside the frozen creek. Rose, the raccoon, was instructing her six young ones in the art of washing their paws. The water was exceedingly cold, yet the babes were enjoying themselves. 

"Rose, my bare legs and bare toes are so cold, may I please borrow a pair of your socks?" begged Luna. 

Rose laughed heartily. "Silly Luna, I do not have socks. Look at my legs and feet. They are covered with thick, warm fur. I'm sorry I cannot help you. Go visit the humans. Sometimes I tip over their garbage cans at night when I am looking for food. Once I saw a pair of socks." 

Luna harboured a great fear of humans. Her grandmother and mother had cautioned her against them. She had been informed that some humans are cruel and harm hawks. Her feet were so cold that to grip tree branches became difficult. She resolved to be brave. She flew to the farmhouse upon the great hill. Upon alighting upon the roof, she beheld something astounding. She perceived socks! In the late autumn, Henrietta the human had placed laundry outdoors to dry and had neglected to retrieve one small pair of socks. The socks dangled from the clothesline, secured by two wooden pins. Luna employed her powerful beak to sever the pins. She donned the socks and then returned to her home in the vast tree. Upon her arrival, her feet were warm and dry. Luna felt exceedingly happy.

Story: CHAPTER XII. TRANSFORMATION



'Well, now for the second stage of our guardianship!' said Aunt Ada, as the two sisters sat over the fire after Valetta had gone to bed. 'Fergus comes back to-morrow, and Gillian---when?'

'She does not seem quite certain, for there is to be a day or two at Brompton with this delightful Geraldine, so that she may see her grandmother---also Mr. Clement Underwood's church, and the Merchant of Venice---an odd mixture of ecclesiastics and dissipations.'

'I wonder whether she will be set up by it.'

'So do I! They are all remarkably good people; but then good people do sometimes spoil the most of all, for they are too unselfish to snub. And on the other hand, seeing the world sometimes has the wholesome effect of making one feel small---'

'My dear Jenny!'

'Oh! I did not mean you, who are never easily effaced; but I was thinking of youthful bumptiousness, fostered by country life and elder sistership.'

'Certainly, though Valetta is really much improved, Gillian has not been as pleasant as I expected, especially during the latter part of the time.'

'Query, was it her fault or mine, or the worry of the examination, or all three?'

'Perhaps you did superintend a little too much at first. More than modern independence was prepared for, though I should not have expected recalcitration in a young Lily; but I think there was more ruffling of temper and more reserve than I can quite understand.'

'It has not been a success. As dear old Lily would have said, "My dream has vanished," of a friend in the younger generation, and now it remains to do the best I can for her in the few weeks that are left, before we have her dear mother again.'

Story: CHAPTER V--CLIPSTONE FRIENDS 



"What idle progeny succeed To chase the rolling circle's speed, Or urge the flying ball."--GRAY. 

The afternoon at Clipstone proved a success. Gillian was in attendance, and each individual discovered congenial companions. Lady Merrifield's sister, Miss Mohun, promptly engaged Miss Prescott as an assistant in the manifold charitable undertakings required in the neglected district of Arnscombe, where Mr. Earl lacked a wife, and the farm ladies were indifferent; but their conference was interrupted by Mysie, who hastened to claim Miss Prescott for a game of croquet. "Uncle Redgie was so glad to see the hoops come into fashion again," and Vera and Paula were scarcely acquainted with the game, having always played at lawn tennis; but they were eager to learn, since Uncle Redgie was a very fine-looking retired General, and there was a youth besides, grown to manly stature; and one boy, at home for Easter, who, having no taste for croquet, went with Primrose to show Thekla the tame menagerie, where a mungoose, invariably called Raki raki, was the most recent acquisition. She was likewise shown the kittens of the beloved Begum, and received as a gift Phoebus, a tabby with a sage countenance and a head marked like a Greek lyre, destined to be moved to the Goyle in due course. 

"If Sister will let me have it," said Thekla. 

"Of course she will," said Primrose. "Mysie says she is so jolly." 

"Dear me! all the girls at our school said she was a regular Old Maid." 

"What shocking bad form!" exclaimed Primrose. "Just like cads of girls," muttered Fergus, unheard; for Thekla continued--"Why, they said she must be our maiden aunt, instead of our sister."

Story: Endemism denotes the condition whereby a species is peculiar to a defined geographic location, such as an island, nation, country, or other specified zone, or habitat type; organisms that are indigenous to a place are not deemed endemic if they are found elsewhere. The extreme opposite of endemism is cosmopolitan distribution. An alternative term for a species that is endemic is precinctive, which applies to species (and subspecific categories) that are restricted to a defined geographical area.

The word "endemic" is derived from New Latin "endēmicus", from Greek ενδήμος, "endēmos", meaning "native". "Endēmos" is formed of "en" signifying "in", and "dēmos" signifying "the people". The term "precinctive" has been suggested by certain scientists, and was first employed in botany by MacCaughey in 1917. It is equivalent to "endemism". "Precinction" was perhaps first used by Frank and McCoy. "Precinctive" appears to have been coined by David Sharp when describing the Hawaiian fauna in 1900: "I use the word precinctive in the sense of 'confined to the area under discussion' ... 'precinctive forms' means those forms that are confined to the area specified." That definition excludes artificial confinement of examples by humans in distant botanical gardens or zoological parks.

Physical, climatic, and biological factors can contribute to endemism. The orange-breasted sunbird is exclusively found in the fynbos vegetation zone of southwestern South Africa. Story: CHAPTER VIII

"I AM WEARY OF A HOPELESS LOVE"

Paul and Arthur maintained a bachelor residence in Mayfair; that is to say, Paul had purchased it and was the sole proprietor, while Arthur availed himself thereof whenever he could obtain leave from his regiment. It was here that Paul discovered his brother on the morning of his arrival in London.

They shook hands in silence; Paul did not wish to speak for the moment. His brother's appearance had overcome him. Though it was one o'clock, he was still in his dressing-gown, with sunken, pale cheeks, save for one bright spot, and with faint, dark rims beneath his eyes. A pile of blue papers and several ominous envelopes lay upon the table before him, and Paul could not refrain from observing the intense pallor of the hand which rested there.

"I wish you would let a fellow know what time you were coming," Arthur said, rather peevishly, yet with an attempt at a smile. "I didn't expect you till evening, so I was having a shack before dressing. I was late last night!"

Paul dismissed his gravity, in so far as possible, and stood with his hands in his pockets, leaning against the mantel-piece. He heartily disliked the role of mentor, and he did not wish to assume it unless compelled.

"It was beastly early to get up," he said, "but the connection at Normanton is so much better. One has to wait two hours by the late train, and Normanton is such a hole. I don't know that I should have come up to town at all, just yet," he continued after a slight pause, "only that I'm on the committee at the club this term, you know, and I haven't attended a single meeting yet. Besides, I promised Westover to put him up this time, and the half-yearly meeting's to-morrow, you know. Got any engagement? If not, you might dine with me there. Always a full night election time, you know!"

Sales outlets and channels are also likely to vary from China, where half of all condoms are bought by women.

Story: CHAPTER XVI. THE SUPREME SACRIFICE 

THROUGH the balance of the day and all during the long night Billy Byrne swung along his lonely way, retracing the familiar steps of the journey which had conveyed Barbara Harding and himself to the little island in the turbulent river. 

Just prior to dawn he arrived at the edge of the clearing situated behind the dwelling of the late Oda Yorimoto. Within the silent village, he was certain that the two prisoners were held. 

During the long march he had repeatedly considered all that the success of his rash venture would mean to him. Of all those who might conceivably stand between him and the woman he loved--the woman who had just acknowledged that she loved him--these two men were the most to be feared. 

Billy Byrne did not for one instant believe that Anthony Harding would view the Grand Avenue mucker with favor as a prospective son-in-law. And then there was Mallory! He was sure that Barbara had loved this man, and now should he be restored to her as from the grave, it seemed little doubt but that the old love would be aroused in the girl's breast. The truth of the matter was that Billy Byrne could not conceive the truth of the testimony of his own ears--even now he scarce dared believe that the wonderful Miss Harding loved him--him, the despised mucker! 

But the depth of the man's love for the girl, and the genuineness of his new-found character were proven beyond question by the relentless severity with which he put away every thought of himself and the consequences to him in the matter he had undertaken.

Story: CHAPTER VIII 

A SCENE IN THE GYMNASIUM 

Lew Flapp spoke in a voice so loud and overbearing that a crowd gathered in the corner where the punching-apparatus was placed. 

"What's up?" asked more than one cadet. 

"Lew Flapp and Dick Rover are going to try to beat each other at punching the bag," was the report. 

"Rover will have to do his best then. Flapp is a prime one at bag punching. It's about the only thing he can do real well." 

"This isn't a fair contest," put in another student. "Flapp took lessons from a man who used to do bag-punching on the vaudeville stage." 

"If that's so I wouldn't try to beat him, if I was Dick Rover." 

Dick heard some of this talk, yet said nothing. He was soon ready for the trial; and stepping up to the punching-bag, he began to undo the top strap. 

"That bag is all right," blustered Lew Flapp. 

"Yes--for you," answered Dick. "But you must remember, I am not quite so tall. I must have it an inch lower." 

"It seems to me you are mighty particular." 

"I have a right to be. When you do your punching you can raise the bag as high as you please." 

"That's the talk," came from several standing near. 

By this time Larry was upon the floor again, and he came up to learn what Dick was doing. 

"Dick, they tell me he is the best bag-puncher here," whispered Larry. 

"I can't help it."

It must not be supposed that such a history of Guy's mind was expressed by himself, or understood by Mrs. Edmonstone; but she saw enough to guess at his character, to perceive the sort of guidance he needed, and to be doubly interested in him. The present question concerning the horse was, in her opinion, unfortunate; for, although Guy had exercised great self-denial, it was no wonder that Philip was annoyed. Mr. Edmonstone's vexation was soon over. As soon as she had persuaded him that there had been no offence, he strove to say with a good grace that it was very proper, and told Guy he would be a thorough book-worm and tremendous scholar, which Guy took as an excellent joke. 

Philip had resolved to be forbearing, and to say no more about it. On his part Guy had no idea of the trouble he had caused; so, after bestowing his thanks in a gay, off-hand way, which Philip thought the worst feature of the case, he did his best to bring Hecuba back into his mind, drive the hunters out of it, and appease the much-aggrieved William of Deloraine.

Story: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun, and the largest in the Solar System. It is a giant planet with a mass one-thousandth that of the Sun, but two and a half times that of all the other planets in the Solar System combined. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; the other two giant planets, Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. Jupiter has been known to astronomers since antiquity. The Romans named it after their god Jupiter. When viewed from the Earth, Jupiter can reach an apparent magnitude of −2.94; it is bright enough for its reflected light to cast shadows, and it is on average the third-brightest object in the night sky after the Moon and Venus.

Jupiter is primarily composed of hydrogen, with a quarter of its mass being helium, though helium comprises only about a tenth of the number of molecules. It may also have a rocky core of heavier elements, but like the other giant planets, Jupiter lacks a well-defined solid surface. Because of its rapid rotation, the planet's shape is that of an oblate spheroid; it has a slight but noticeable bulge around the equator. The outer atmosphere is visibly segregated into several bands at different latitudes, resulting in turbulence and storms along their interacting boundaries. A prominent result is the Great Red Spot, a giant storm that is known to have existed since at least the 17th century, when it was first seen by telescope. Surrounding Jupiter is a faint planetary ring system and a powerful magnetosphere. Jupiter has at least 69 moons, including the four large Galilean moons discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610. Ganymede, the largest of these, has a diameter greater than that of the planet Mercury.

Story: CHAPTER XIII. 

THE LETTER. 

There could be no question that the company of Ninety-four were highly delighted by the news which Seth had brought concerning his progress. 

It was as though each man felt himself personally complimented by Mr. Fernald for advancing the amateur so rapidly; and all united in the declaration that "Josh was a right good fellow." 

Seth was in the highest degree excited. He had expected that his friends of Ninety-four would be pleased to learn of his good fortune, but he had never fancied that they could be so deeply interested; and now he began to understand what a gloom might be cast over the company should he fail in this attempt to gain a foothold in the Department. 

'Lish Davis would not be content until the boy had given an exhibition of what he had learned in the matter of gymnastic exercises during the morning; and when this had been brought to a close amid the applause of all present, the driver said, in a tone of satisfaction: 

"You're getting on in great shape, Amateur, and if nothing happens to give you a pull-back, ought'er be well up in the drill 'twixt now and a year from to-day. Josh Fernald has the name of being precious hard on them as comes under him for instruction; but I've always allowed he'd boost along mighty fast any one who struck his fancy. He must have seen that you were in earnest, young fellow, for when I talked with him the best promise I could get was that he'd look you over in the course of a month or two."

Story: CHAPTER XXVI 

THE JUDGMENT OF DOMITIAN 

Two hours having elapsed, Caleb, in a ferment of rage, sat brooding in the office adjoining the warehouse he had leased. At that instant, he harboured but a single desire—to put to death his successful rival, Marcus. That Marcus had escaped and returned to Rome was beyond all question. He, one of the wealthiest patricians in that city, had furnished the enormous sum which enabled old Nehushta to purchase the coveted Pearl-Maiden in the slave-ring. Thenceforth, his newly acquired property had been conveyed to this house, where he awaited her arrival. Thus, then, was the end of their long rivalry; for this had Caleb fought, toiled, schemed, and suffered. Rather than permit such an outcome, in that dark hour of his soul, he would have seen her cast to the foul Domitian, for Domitian, at least, she would have hated, whereas Marcus, as he knew, she loved.

Now, there remained nothing but revenge. Revenge he must have, but by what means? He might follow Marcus and murder him; only then his own life would be placed in jeopardy, since he knew well the fate that awaited the foreigner, and most especially the Jew, who dared to lift his hand against a Roman noble. Moreover, if he hired others to do the work, they might bear witness against him. Now, Caleb did not wish to die; life seemed the only good that he had left. Furthermore, while he lived, he might still win Miriam—after his rival had ceased to live. Doubtless, then, she would be sold with his other slaves, and he could buy her at the rate such tarnished goods command. No, he would do nothing to run himself into danger. He would wait, and watch his opportunity.

Story: CHAPTER XXX. 

THE MEETING FOR RAIN. 

Meanwhile the Auld Lichts were assembled in church, awaiting their minister; the attendance was considerable, since nearly every well in Thrums had been drawn dry by eager hands. Yet not all were present to implore divine rain for their own benefit. Old Charles Yuill sat in his pew, having dreamt thrice that he would perish with the drought; and Bell Christison had come, though her husband lay dead at home, and she deemed it no longer of consequence to her how affairs proceeded in the world. 

To one who bears no affection for that small congregation, their waiting might have appeared placid. But likely so artless a woman as Meggy Rattray could have misled one into supposing that, because her eyes were lowered, she took no heed of who placed the three-penny-bit in the plate. A few men, chiefly farmers with their gaze upon the windows, were unaware that the bell tolled beyond its customary time, yet all the women at least were wondering. They knew better, however, than to betray their thoughts by their countenances, and none sought to meet another's gaze. The men looked steadfastly at their hats upon the seats before them. Even when Hendry Munn, instead of proceeding to the pulpit with the large Bible in his grasp, advanced to the plate and signaled to Peter Tosh, the elder, that his presence was required in the vestry, one could not have divined how every woman there, save Bell Christison, wished herself to be Peter Tosh. Peter was so taken aback that he merely gaped at Hendry, until suddenly he perceived that his five daughters were enraged with him, whereupon he snatched his hat and staggered to the vestry with his mouth agape. His boots cheeped throughout the passage, but no one looked up.

Story: Chapter IX.--THE AUSTRIAN-SAXON ARMY INVADES SILESIA, ACROSS THE MOUNTAINS.

Valori, who was to be of Friedrich's Campaign this Year, came posting off directly in rear of the glorious news of Fontenoy; he found Friedrich at Camenz, rather in spirits than otherwise; and lodged pleasantly with Abbot Tobias and him, till the Campaign should begin. Two things surprised Valori: first, the great strength, impregnable as it were, to which Neisse has been brought since he saw it last,--superlative condition of that Fortress, and of the Army itself, as it gathers daily more and more about Frankenstein here:--and then secondly, and contrariwise, the strangely neglected posture of mountainous or Upper Silesia, given up to Pandours. Quite submerged, in a manner: Margraf Karl lies quiet among them at Jagerndorf, "eating his magazine;" General Hautcharmoi (Winterfeld's late chief in that Wurben affair), with his small Detachment, still hovers about in those Ratibor parts, "with the Strong Towns to fall-back upon," or has in effect fallen back accordingly; and nothing is done to coerce the Pandours at all. While Prince Karl and Weissenfels are daily coming on, in force 100,000, their intention certain; force, say, about 100,000 regular! Very singular to Valori.

"Sire, will not you dispute the Passes, then?" asks Valori, amazed: "Not defend your Mountain rampart, then?" "MON CHER; the Mountain rampart is three or four hundred miles long; there are twelve or twenty practicable roads through it. One is kept in darkness, too; endless Pandour doggery shutting out your daylight:--ill defending such a rampart," answers Friedrich. "But how, then," persists Valori; "but--?" "One day the King answered me," says Valori, "'MON AMI, if you want to get the mouse, don't shut, the trap; leave the trap open (ON LAISSE LA SOURICIERE OUVERTE)!'" Which was a beam of light to the inquiring thought of Valori, a military man of some intelligence. [See VALORI, i. 222, 224, 228.]

Story: Chapter IX.--THE AUSTRIAN-SAXON ARMY INVADES SILESIA, ACROSS THE MOUNTAINS. 

Valori, who was to be of Friedrich's Campaign this Year, came hastening off directly in rear of the glorious news of Fontenoy; found Friedrich at Camenz, rather in spirits than otherwise; and resided agreeably with Abbot Tobias and him, till the Campaign should begin. Two things surprised Valori: first, the vast strength, impregnable as it were, to which Neisse had been brought since he saw it last,--excellent condition of that Fortress, and of the Army itself, as it gathered daily more and more about Frankenstein here:--and then secondly, and contrariwise, the singularly neglected posture of mountainous or Upper Silesia, abandoned to the Pandours. In a manner, quite submerged: Margraf Karl lay quiet among them at Jagerndorf, "eating his magazine;" General Hautcharmoi (Winterfeld's late chief in that Wurben affair), with his small Detachment, still hovered about in those Ratibor parts, "with the Strong Towns to fall-back upon," or had in effect fallen back accordingly; and nothing had been done to coerce the Pandours at all. While Prince Karl and Weissenfels were daily coming on, with a force of 100,000, their intention certain; force, say, about 100,000 regular! This was very singular to Valori. 

"Sire, will not you dispute the Passes, then?" asks Valori, amazed: "Not defend your Mountain rampart, then?" "MON CHER; the Mountain rampart is three or four hundred miles long; there are twelve or twenty practicable roads through it. One is kept in darkness, too; endless Pandour doggery shutting out your daylight:--ill defending such a rampart," answers Friedrich. "But how, then," persists Valori; "but--?" Story: CHAPTER VIII. 

HOSTAGE. 

The revolution of Todos Santos had, to all appearances, been carried out as peacefully as the gentle Liberator of Quinquinambo could have wished. Two pronunciamientos, rudely printed and posted in the Plaza, were saluted by the fickle garrison of one hundred men, who, however, immediately reappointed their old commander as Generalissimo under the new regime; this seemed to leave nothing to be desired. A surging mob of vacant and wondering peons, bearing a singular resemblance to the wild cattle and horses which intermingled with them in blind and unceasing movement across the Plaza and up the hilly street, and seemingly as incapable of self-government, were alternately dispersed and stampeded or allowed to gather again as occasion required. Some of these heterogeneous bands were afterwards found, the revolution having been accomplished, gazing stupidly on the sea, or ruminating in bovine wantonness on the glacis before the Presidio. 

Eleanor Keene, who, with her countrywomen, had been hurried to the refuge of the Mission, was more disturbed and excited at the prospect of meeting Hurlstone again than by any terror of the insurrection. Yet Hurlstone was not there, and Father Esteban received her with a coldness which she could not attribute entirely to her countrymen's supposed sympathy with the insurgents. When Richard Keene, who would not leave his sister until he had seen her safe under the Mission walls, ventured at her suggestion to ask after the American recluse, Father Esteban replied dryly that, being a Christian gentleman, Hurlstone was the only one who had the boldness to seek out the American filibuster Perkins, on his own ship, and remonstrate with him for his unholy crusade. For the old priest had already become aware of Hurlstone's blunder, and he hated Eleanor as the primary cause of the trouble; but for her, Diego would be still with him in this emergency.

The revolution of Todos Santos appeared to have been accomplished with a peaceableness that the gentle Liberator of Quinquinambo could scarcely have desired. Some of these heterogeneous bands were afterwards found--the revolution accomplished--gazing stupidly on the sea, or ruminating in bovine wantonness on the glacis before the Presidio. 

Eleanor Keene, who with her countrywomen had been hurried to the refuge of the Mission, was more disturbed and excited at the prospect of meeting Hurlstone again than by any terror of the insurrection. Story: ChiChi weighs only 13 pounds. "He's so tiny,I can carry him with one hand," says Mary Lane."Most people see him and think he's useless." 

But last October,ChiChi proved to be more than just a pretty face. Mary and her husband,Rick,were relaxing on the beach one afternoon while on vacation in North Carolina's Outer Banks.As usual,ChiChi was lying on his blanket in his own little beach chair. 

"We had our noses buried in books,"recalls Rick,"when suddenly the dog became extremely uneasy. His bark was different from anything we had heard before.And he would not let us ignore him." 

ChiChi ran back and forth in front of his chair as if to run down the beach.The Lanes sat up to see two elderly women in the ocean,about 100 yards down the beach and 10 feet off shore.One was on her back,her head under the waves.The other was struggling hard to keep her friend's head above the surface. 

The Lanes rushed across the sand and into the surf. Rick went to the woman in danger of drowning,while Mary held fast on to the other one and pulled her up on the beach."Then I went back to help Rick," Mary says."The sand dropped off steeply,and a riptide was beating the woman under. She was completely helpless." 

Not getting well from recent knee surgery,the woman had been unable to turn over or push herself up."Her friend had been in danger too," Mary says."The waves were pushing her around. There's no way she could have held on much longer." 

The women hadn't called out for help. "They were struggling so hard that there was no time for screaming," Mary recalls."But ChiChi had sensed their danger." 

Duty done,ChiChi was back in his chair,asleep,by the time the two women were on dry ground and the Lanes had returned to their blankets.Luckily,the women were fine,though shaken.They thanked the Lanes for saving their lives. 

Back home in Greensboro,North Carolina,the Lanes ordered a special collar with the words "Hero Dog" on it.

Story: CHAPTER II 

THE RULERS OF FRANCE 

A great bustle prevailed in the corridors and kitchens of the old château. M. le Chef, the only true rival of the immortal Vatel, was in white cap and apron; calm and self-possessed as a field-marshal at the moment of victory, and surrounded by a host of scullions and wenches, he directed the operations of dishing-up, which constituted the crowning glory of his arduous labours. Pies and patties, haunches of venison, trout and carp from the Rhine, were placed upon dishes of gold and silver, and adorned with tasteful ornaments of a truly architectural beauty and monumental proportions. These were then handed over to the footmen, who, resplendent in gorgeous liveries of scarlet and azure, hurried along the marble passages, carrying the masterpieces of culinary art to the banqueting-hall beyond; whilst the butlers, more sedate and dignified in sober garb of puce or brown, stalked along in stately repose, bearing the huge tankards and crystal jugs. 

All of the best that the fine old Château d'Aumont could provide was being requisitioned that night, since M. le Duc and Mlle. Lydie, his daughter, were giving a farewell banquet to Charles Edward Stuart, by the grace of God—if not by the will of the people—King of Great Britain and Ireland and all her dependencies beyond the seas. 

For him speeches were made, toasts drunk, and glasses raised; for him the ducal veneries had been ransacked, and the ducal cellars shorn of their most ancient possessions; for him M. le Chef had raged and stormed for five hours, expending the sweat of his brow and the intricacies of his brain; for him the scullions' backs had smarted, and the wenches' cheeks had glowed—all to do honour to the only rightful King of England, about to quit the hospitable land of France in order to conquer that island kingdom which his grandfather had lost.

Story: CHAPTER XIII. 

A JOYFUL MEETING. 

It is exceedingly probable that one might have searched throughout New York City that night and not discovered a happier household than that of Mrs. Green's. Paul was so exceedingly happy in the thought that he was going back to Chicago, where, even though he could not see his parents, he would find relatives and friends, that he could speak of little else. Even the theatre was forgotten by him; for when Mopsey spoke of the need of obtaining another boy to take his place in the dramatic company, he hardly gave the matter a thought, except to express his hope that they would make a great deal of money from it. And Paul's partners were happy, more happy than they could possibly have been by any other expenditure of their money; Paul's pleasure was reflected upon them to such a degree that they became almost as excited as he before the evening concluded. 

The good Mrs. Green alternately laughed and wept, until she appeared to realize that such nervousness was not altogether suitable to the occasion, and then she occupied herself with reading one of the papers Ben had brought home. 

Master Treat had devoted so much time to the good work which he had carried through with such success, and then had given so much greater attention to the boy he intended to surprise than to the sale of his wares, that, instead of assisting Johnny as had been his purpose when he took some of his papers to sell, he proved a hindrance, with the result that Mrs. Green had three evening papers to read, while Messrs. Jones and Treat had been "stuck" with precisely that number.

Story: Tom Brennan was employed in a Philadelphia office building when he perceived a black bag. The bag contained a volume. This fortuitous discovery concluded a 12-day search by the Library Company of Philadelphia for a historical treasure-a 120-page diary kept 190 years ago by Deborah Logan, "a woman who knew everybody in her day," as James Green, the librarian, informed the magazine American Libraries. The greater portion of the diary constitutes a record of significant events in Philadelphia. It also contains a depiction of British soldiers burning Washington, D.C. during the war of 1812. She portrays President James Madison on horseback as "perfectly shaking with fear" during those disturbed times. George Washington, she relates, mistook her for the wife of a French gentleman and commended her excellent English. The affair of the lost book commenced on September 4 when Cory Luxmoore arrived from England to deliver the diary of his ancestor to the Library Company, which he and his wife regarded as the most fitting repository for the diary. Green informed American Libraries that he had had the diary in his possession "about five minutes" when Luxmoore reclaimed it, having promised to display it to one other individual. Upon returning to his hotel after exhibiting the precious volume to Green, Luxmoore was astonished to discover that he had abandoned it in the taxi. Without hesitation, Green commenced calling every taxi company in the city, with no success. "I've felt sick since then," Luxmoore told reporters. According to Green, no person has as yet ascertained how the diary came to the office building. Tom Brennan received a reward of $ 1,000, Philadelphia acquired another treasure for its history, and Luxmoore told reporters, "It's wonderful news. I'm on high."

It was late at night before Blois was reached; and having alighted at the Aigle d'Or, they engaged a private room.

"Even the Duke of Chateaurouge will be satisfied," Ronald said, "that his schemes have failed, and that no more can be done just at present. It will be a bitter blow to him when those scoundrels, on their return to Paris, report their utter failure, for he must have considered it impossible that we could escape from the toils he had laid for us. I only wish that we had clear evidence that he is the author of these attempts. If so, I would go straight with Marshal Saxe and lay an accusation against him before the king; but however certain we may feel about it, we have really nothing to connect him with the affair, and it would be madness to accuse a king's favourite unless one could prove absolutely the truth of what one says. However, I hope some day that I shall get even with him. It will not be my fault if I do not."

That evening Ronald and his mother debated what would be the best course to pursue on the morrow; and it was finally agreed that Malcolm should present himself at the prison with the order of release, while they themselves should remain at the hotel, to which Malcolm was to bring Colonel Leslie after having broken to him the news that his wife and son were both awaiting him. The shock, in any case, of sudden liberty would be a severe one; and the meeting with his attached comrade would serve as a preparation for that with his wife.

I only wish that we had clear evidence that he is the author of these attempts. If so, I would go straight with Marshal Saxe and lay an accusation against him before the king; but however certain we may feel about it, we have really nothing to connect him with the affair, and it would be madness to accuse a king's favourite unless one could prove absolutely the truth of what one says. However, I hope some day that I shall get even with him. It will not be my fault if I do not."

The snowstorm proved so severe that for three days the party at Professor Jeffer's cabin were completely stormbound. At one point Andy and Chet ventured out--in an endeavor to bring in the dead moose--but were unable to accomplish their object. 

During the time spent at the cabin, the boys became well acquainted with Barwell Dawson, and found the hunter and explorer a person much to their liking. Although he was rich and well educated, he did not act as though he considered himself above them. He took a lively interest in all they had to tell, and knew how to "draw them out," so that, almost before he was aware of it, Andy had related the details of his troubles with his shiftless Uncle Si and with the mysterious Mr. A. Q. Hopton. 

"More than likely that fellow, Hopton, will bear close watching," said Barwell Dawson. "If he is a sharper--and it looks as if he might be--he will try to swindle both you and your uncle. It was very unwise for your uncle to try to do business with him without seeing a lawyer." 

"Uncle Si wanted to get the money without my knowing it," answered Andy, bitterly. He was glad to open his heart to one who could understand him. 

"I believe you--and that is not to your uncle's credit. You say he is shiftless and lazy?" 

"Very--and everybody around here knows it." 

"Then he is not fit to be your guardian."

The snowstorm proved so severe that for three days the party at Professor Jeffer's cabin were wholly stormbound. Once Andy and Chet ventured out in an effort to bring the dead moose in, but were unable to accomplish their object. 

During their sojourn at the cabin, the boys became very well acquainted with Barwell Dawson, and found the hunter and explorer a person exceedingly to their liking. Though he was rich and well educated, he did not act as though he considered himself above them. He took a lively interest in all they had to relate, and knew how to "draw them out," so that, almost before he knew it, Andy had detailed the circumstances of his troubles with his shiftless Uncle Si and with the mysterious Mr. A. Q. Hopton. 

"More than likely that fellow, Hopton, will bear close watching," said Barwell Dawson. "If he is a sharper--and it looks as if he might be--he will try to swindle both you and your uncle. It was very unwise for your uncle to try to do business with him without seeing a lawyer." 

"Uncle Si wanted to get the money without my knowing it," answered Andy, bitterly. He was glad to open his heart to somebody who could understand him. 

"I believe you--and that is not to your uncle's credit. You say he is shiftless and lazy?" 

"Very--and everybody around here knows it." 

"Then he is not fit to be your guardian."

Story: Sarah's New Kitty

"Meow."

Sarah's eyes opened wide when she heard that sound coming from the basket her mother was holding.

"Mama, what's that sound? It sounds like a kitty!" she said to her mother as she tried to reach the basket, which was held up too high for her grasp.

"Sarah," her mother said, "remember I told you that maybe we can get a pet if you could take good care of it? Well, you're seven years old now and I think you're ready for a special present."

Sarah's mother set the basket on the floor. Sarah sank to her knees with a broad grin upon her face. Slowly she lifted the yellow kitty and held its soft little body next to her own.

She gave the kitty a little kiss; then she rubbed its head and neck. Soon it began making gentle sounds. "Why is the kitty making those funny sounds?" she asked her mother. "Oh, that's called purring. It's the sound kittens make when they're happy," her mother said.

"Can I give it a name?" Sarah asked.

"Sure. It's a girl kitty, but choose any name you like." her mother said.

Sarah thought upon the matter as her mother got two small bowls and placed them on the floor. She put water in one bowl and kitten food in the other. "Okay, Sarah. Let's see if the kitty is hungry."

Sarah put the kitty on the floor, and it walked over to the food bowl. It quickly began to eat.

Sarah laughed at the kitten and said, "I know. I'm going to name you Kitty."

His small size is a distinct advantage in such a game. But Lightfoot the Deer is big. He is one of the largest of the people who live in the Green Forest. Being so big，it was not easy to hide.

Furthermore，a hunter with a terrible gun does not have to come close in order to kill. Lightfoot knew all this as he waited for the coming of the hunter of whom Sammy Jay had warned him. Many lessons had he learned in the hunting season of the year before，and he remembered every one. He knew that to forget even one might cost him his life. And so，standing motionless behind a tangle of fallen trees，Lightfoot listened and watched.
